title: The risk management process
blurb: Name the stages of the risk management process in order and say what happens at each one.
question: A school building project has just held a risk workshop and produced a long list of possible problems. The project manager wants to start buying insurance straight away. Which stage of the risk management process has been skipped, and what comes after it?

teach.h: Four stages, always in this order
teach.body: The PFQ syllabus describes a typical risk management process in four stages: IDENTIFICATION, ANALYSIS, RESPONSE and CLOSURE. First find the risks, then size them up, then decide and carry out what to do about them, and finally close them when they no longer apply. The APM Body of Knowledge (7th edition) also puts an INITIATE step at the front: agreeing how risk will be managed on this project, recorded in a risk management plan.

teach.body: A project might identify dozens of risks but has limited time and money to deal with them. Analysis assesses each one's probability and impact so the team can prioritise, spending effort on the risks that matter most. Choosing responses before analysis is like treating patients in the order they walked in rather than by how ill they are.

The response stage is more than picking a strategy. The team chooses and plans a proportionate response, assigns a RISK OWNER (the person accountable for managing that risk) plus any action owners, then implements the actions and monitors whether they are working. If a response is not working, the risk is reassessed and the response revised.

teach.h: Closure is more than ticking a box
teach.body: A risk is closed when it can no longer happen (the moment has passed), when it has occurred and is being handled as an issue, or when it no longer matters. Closure means reviewing how effective the responses were and capturing lessons for future projects. At the end of the project, the risk management process itself is closed.

teach.note: A new risk spotted mid-project goes back to Identification: the process is iterative, not a one-off.

teach.text: Don't mix up the two processes in LO7. The RISK process is identification, analysis, response, closure. 'Escalate to the sponsor' belongs to the ISSUE resolution process, not the risk process. And 'response' is not the same as 'analysis': scoring a risk is analysis; deciding what to do is response.

items: Stages in order: identification, analysis, response, closure (BoK7 adds 'initiate' first).
Identification finds and describes risks; analysis assesses probability and impact to prioritise.
Response: choose a response, assign a risk owner, implement and monitor.
Closure: close passed risks, review how well responses worked, capture lessons.
The process repeats throughout the project as new risks emerge.

summary: You can now name the four stages of the risk management process in order (identification, analysis, response, closure) and say what happens at each. You also know that it is a repeating process, and that BoK7 adds an initiate step to agree the approach first.

A.q: Which sequence shows the stages of a typical risk management process in the correct order?
A.why: Risks are first identified, then analysed, then responded to, and finally closed.

whyNot.0: You cannot analyse a risk before it has been identified.
whyNot.1: Responses should follow analysis, so effort goes to the most significant risks.
whyNot.3: A response cannot be chosen for a risk that has not yet been identified.

A.q: At which stage of the risk management process are risks assessed for probability and impact?
A.why: Analysis assesses each risk's probability and impact so that risks can be prioritised.

whyNot.0: Closure deals with risks that have passed or occurred.
whyNot.2: Response decides and carries out actions, using the analysis as its input.
whyNot.3: Identification finds and describes risks; it does not size them.

A.q: During which stage is a risk owner normally assigned?
A.why: In the response stage a response is chosen and a risk owner (plus action owners) is assigned to implement and monitor it.

whyNot.0: Identification records the risk; ownership is confirmed when the response is planned.
whyNot.1: By closure the risk has passed, so assigning an owner would be too late.
whyNot.2: Analysis scores and prioritises; it does not allocate responsibility for actions.

B.q: Why is risk analysis carried out before responses are chosen?
options: So effort goes to the most significant risks
So every risk can be closed immediately
So the sponsor can approve the issue log
So the budget can be fixed before any planning
B.why: Analysis prioritises risks by probability and impact, so the team can focus responses on the risks that matter most.

whyNot.1: Risks are closed when they pass or occur, not straight after analysis.
whyNot.2: The issue log belongs to issue management, not the risk process.
whyNot.3: Analysis informs plans and contingency; it does not exist to fix the budget first.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the risk management process?
B.why: Escalation to the sponsor is a stage of the issue resolution process, not the risk management process.

whyNot.0: Identification is the first stage of the risk process.
whyNot.2: Response is the third stage of the risk process.
whyNot.3: Closure is the final stage of the risk process.

B.q: Midway through delivery, a team spots a new threat that has never been recorded. What should happen?
options: Close it, as planning is already complete
Ignore it until the next phase gate
Treat it as an issue for the sponsor
Identify, analyse and respond to it
B.why: The process is iterative: a new risk is identified, then analysed and responded to like any other, whenever it appears.

whyNot.0: Closing a live risk would leave it unmanaged.
whyNot.1: Waiting removes the chance to act early, which is the point of risk management.
whyNot.2: It has not happened yet, so it is a risk, not an issue.

C.q:
A risk that a heatwave would delay roof works has passed, as the roof is now complete. Which TWO actions belong to the closure stage?
1. Close the risk in the register
2. Re-score its probability
3. Review how well the response worked
4. Assign a new action owner
C.why: Closure means formally closing risks that have passed and reviewing how effective the responses were, capturing lessons.

whyNot.0: Closing is right, but re-scoring a risk that can no longer happen is pointless.
whyNot.1: Re-scoring and new owners belong to live risks, not closed ones.
whyNot.3: Reviewing is right, but a passed risk needs no new action owner.

C.q: According to APM's Body of Knowledge (7th edition), what happens before risks are identified?
options: The approach to risk is agreed and planned
All risks are transferred to an insurer
The issue log is reviewed by the sponsor
Contingency is spent on the largest risks
C.why: BoK7 places an 'initiate' step first: the approach to managing risk is agreed and recorded in a risk management plan.

whyNot.1: Transfer is a response to particular threats, chosen later and not for every risk.
whyNot.2: The issue log belongs to issue management, not the start of the risk process.
whyNot.3: Contingency is sized after analysis and drawn down only if needed.

C.q: A project manager puts a planned response into action and checks each week whether it is working. Which stage is this?
C.why: The response stage includes implementing the chosen actions and monitoring whether they are effective.

whyNot.0: Closure comes once the risk has passed; this risk is still live.
whyNot.1: Identification finds risks; this one is already known.
whyNot.3: Analysis assesses probability and impact; it does not carry out actions.

reteach.title: Planning a house extension
reteach.question: A family is adding a kitchen extension. How would they handle what might go wrong (or right) using the same four stages a project uses?

blocks.body: Over coffee they list what might happen: the builder might find old drains, the council might query the plans, steel prices might fall (identification). They decide the drains are the most likely and the most expensive (analysis). They pay for a drain survey and keep £2,000 aside, with Dad in charge of chasing it (response). When the foundations are poured, the drains risk has passed: they cross it off and note to survey early next time (closure).

steps.label:
Act and put
someone in charge

blocks.text: The family did not pay for every possible precaution: they sized the risks first. Analysis before response is what keeps effort and money proportionate.

explain.body: Finding the risks that could affect objectives and describing each one clearly, then recording it (usually in the risk register). It happens at the start and keeps happening throughout the project.

test.q: What is the main aim of the identification stage?
options: To find and record possible risks
To close risks that have passed
test.why: Identification finds the risks that could affect objectives and records them.

whyNot.0: Scoring likelihood is part of analysis.
whyNot.2: Closing passed risks is the closure stage.
whyNot.3: Buying insurance is a transfer response, chosen in the response stage.

explain.body: Assessing each risk's probability and impact so risks can be ranked. Most risks get a qualitative score; the most significant may also get quantitative modelling.

test.q: What does the analysis stage mainly produce?
options: A list of lessons for future projects
A set of named owners for each action
Risks ranked by probability and impact
A signed contract with an insurer
test.why: Analysis produces an assessment of each risk's probability and impact, giving a priority order.

whyNot.0: Lessons are captured mainly at closure.
whyNot.1: Action owners are assigned in the response stage.
whyNot.3: An insurance contract is a transfer response, not an analysis output.

explain.body: Choosing and planning a proportionate response, assigning a risk owner and action owners, then implementing the actions and monitoring them.

test.q: Which activity belongs to the response stage?
options: Holding a brainstorm to list new risks
Scoring risks on a probability grid
Recording lessons after a risk passes
Assigning an owner to carry out actions
test.why: Assigning owners and carrying out the chosen actions is the response stage.

whyNot.0: Brainstorming to list risks is identification.
whyNot.1: Scoring risks on a matrix is analysis.
whyNot.2: Recording lessons after a risk has passed is closure.

explain.body: Closing risks that have passed or occurred, reviewing how effective the responses were, and capturing lessons. At project end the risk process itself is closed.

test.q: A risk can no longer happen because the activity it affected is finished. What should happen to it?
options: It should be escalated as an issue
It should be re-scored as high
It should be left open just in case
test.why: A risk that can no longer occur should be formally closed, with its outcome and any lessons recorded.

whyNot.1: Nothing has gone wrong, so there is no issue to escalate.
whyNot.2: A risk that cannot happen has no probability left to score.
whyNot.3: Leaving dead risks open clutters the register and hides the live ones.
